title: Green ash bowl on the pole lathe
subtitle: A small utility bowl turned from green ash in one session
excerpt: A 15 cm bowl in green ash, turned on a pole lathe with a gouge. Pole-lathe turning is interrupted-cut turning: the tool cuts only on the down stroke. Green ash turns fast, but the bowl must be dried slowly after turning to avoid cracking. An advanced project because it requires a working pole lathe setup.
sourceNotes: Mike Abbott, Green Woodwork (1989), Batsford: technique descriptions for pole-lathe bowl turning; now public record in archival descriptions. Bowl profile derived from traditional Welsh dairy tradition.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.
A human-powered reciprocating lathe driven by a flexible pole that returns the treadle after each down-stroke. The tool cuts on the down-stroke only.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished item is carved or turned.

content.text: A pole lathe bowl is turned from a section of green log, split in half, and mounted with the flat split face to the front. The lathe rotates the blank in an alternating direction: the tool cuts on the down-stroke when the blank rotates into the tool, and lifts clear on the return. This interrupted cutting means the turning is slower than on a power lathe, but it also means a sharp edge and a light touch are more important than power.
Green ash
is the recommended species: it turns readily under a well-set gouge, dries to a stable cream-white bowl, and is food-safe. Advanced project due to the
pole-lathe
setup requirement and the control needed for the interrupted-cut technique.
Before you start turning.
The pole lathe must be properly set up and tensioned before any work begins. A loose drive cord or an incorrectly set tool rest can cause the work to fly off the lathe.
Always stand to the side of the lathe axis, not directly in front, when first mounting and testing the blank.
The gouge should only engage the work on the down-stroke. If the gouge is catching on the return, the tool rest is too far from the work.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Wood
Green ash in the freshly-felled state, from a round section 20 to 22 cm in diameter. Split the round in half with the
blank

section oriented so the pith is not in the centre of the bowl profile. A quarter-split section avoids the pith entirely. The half-log starts at 20 cm long; the finished bowl is 15 cm diameter and 7 cm deep. Sycamore also works well and dries paler than ash.
Method
Step 1: Axe the outside profile

Before mounting on the lathe, rough-shape the outside of the bowl with the carving axe. Remove the corners of the half-log to a rough dome. The axe work should bring the blank close to round so the initial lathe rotation is not violently eccentric.
Step 2: Mount on the lathe

Mount the blank between the pole lathe's drive centre (into the face of the bowl) and the tail centre (into the base of the bowl). Tighten the tail centre until the blank holds firmly with no lateral movement. Set the tool rest 5 mm below the centreline at a distance of 15 mm from the blank surface.
Step 3: Turn the outside

Use the deep-sweep gouge to turn the outside to a smooth dome. Present the tool with the flute (the curved face) at 45 degrees, engaging only the cutting edge, and ride the tool rest. Cuts are made only on the down-stroke; keep the tool moving with the treadle rhythm. Green ash turns easily; shavings should come off as long, damp curls.
Step 4: Hollow the inside

Reverse the blank: the bowl interior now faces outward. Mount again between centres. Use the deep-sweep gouge to clear the interior, working from the rim toward the centre on each down-stroke. Check wall thickness every five minutes with a finger and thumb: 8 to 10 mm is correct at the rim, 12 to 15 mm at the base.
Drying and finishing

Green ash bowls crack if dried too fast. Wrap the finished bowl loosely in newspaper or place it in a paper bag and leave in a cool, dry place for eight to twelve weeks. Check every two weeks. Once dry, apply raw linseed oil to all surfaces. Two coats over two days, wiped surplus each time. Cure for two weeks before food use.

attrs.symptom: The blank is wobbling violently on the lathe
attrs.cause: The tail centre is not tight enough, or the blank is still very far from round.
attrs.fix: Stop the lathe. Tighten the tail centre. If wobble persists, remove the blank and take more material off with the axe before re-mounting.

attrs.cause: Drying was too fast, either from direct sunlight or a heated room.
attrs.fix: Wrap in newspaper and move to a cool space with air movement but no direct heat. A crack can sometimes be stabilised by rubbing raw linseed oil into it on the second day of drying.
